summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a zero-install web app that compares south-pole landing sites and dates by showing where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon. It turns the question of when a site has both power and direct-to-Earth comms into a colour-coded timeline, a sky view, a ranked table and a polar map with lunar vehicles. A readiness checklist covers eight landing challenges. It is built with Visual Studio and Claude, ships as one HTML file on GitHub Pages, and comes with a 6-slide briefing on the challenges and the path to a successful landing.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites near the Moon’s south pole and choose when to land. Planning there is hard because the Sun hangs just above the horizon and Earth is also low in the sky. Existing tools can compute those positions, but their interfaces make quick comparisons difficult. This project makes the comparison fast and visual.

What it does

  • Timeline: shows each site over a 7–120 day window, colour-coded for Sun and Earth both up (power and comms), Sun only, Earth only, or neither.
  • Sky view: a horizon panorama for the selected site and time. It plots the Sun and Earth with their paths across the window, and a slider or play button steps through time.
  • Comparison table: ranks sites by the percentage of time with Sun, Earth and both visible. It also shows the longest dark gap and the longest stretch with no Earth link.
  • South pole map: a polar view with day/night shading that follows the time slider. It marks candidate sites and lunar vehicles: Chandrayaan-3, IM-2 Athena, the crashed Chandrayaan-2 and Luna 25, and the planned Chang’e-7, Blue Moon MK1 and Griffin-1.
  • Landing readiness checklist: eight challenges (power, night survival, comms, outages, landing window, slope, navigation, thermal) with a progress bar. A button jumps to the best landing window.
  • Terrain mask and custom sites: a slider approximates terrain blocking the horizon, and you can add any latitude and longitude.

How it works. The tool computes Sun and Earth directions in the Moon-fixed frame from lunar phase, libration and solar declination. It then converts them to elevation and azimuth for each site. It is a single self-contained index.html with no dependencies, so it runs offline and deploys directly on GitHub Pages.

Tools used. We built the project using Visual Studio and Claude. Claude helped design the model and interface and wrote the code, the documentation and the 6-slide briefing. We edited and ran the code in Visual Studio, and the repo is hosted on GitHub.

Limitations. The ephemeris is a simplified analytic model, accurate to roughly 1–2° and a few hours, and it has not been checked against SPICE or JPL Horizons. The terrain mask is one uniform angle, and the vehicle positions are approximate. It is for education and early planning, not flight-grade analysis.
